The mercury has a way of remembering cold long before the glass does. 

In the high room over the salt marsh, where the wind comes off the shelf with the blunt authority of an iron spade, the columns rise and fall in their wooden casings. There are seven barometers along the north wall. Some are English, mahogany-cased and slender as walking sticks, their vernier scales worn silver by thumbs dead for two centuries. Others are French, bulbous and utilitarian, fitted with siphon tubes that gurgle like sleeping hounds whenever a squall drives through the gap in the headland.

My trade, if it can still be called one, is to keep them honest.

People believe that pressure is a simple thing: the sky sits upon the earth, and the earth bears it. But the air is not a slab of granite. It is a lung, an ocean of thin silk that bunches and stretches. It heaps itself into mountains over the Azores; it tears into long, ragged trenches above the Newfoundland banks. Down here, at the foot of the cliff, the tide does what it must, dragging bladderwrack across the shale twice a day. But up here, we measure the invisible ceiling. We weigh what cannot be held.

To mend a broken tube, you must first master the art of boiling mercury. It is a quiet, deadly business. You sit over a blue spirit flame with an iron ladle, watching the metal shiver. It does not want to be liquid; it wants to be a mirror. It wants to gather itself into a single, impenetrable sphere and roll toward the nearest dark corner. When it boils, the vapor rises colorless and sweet, smelling faintly of old coins and static electricity. Breathe enough of it, and your teeth loosen; breathe a little more, and you begin to converse with people who are not in the room. I keep the sashes thrown open, even in November, while the terns bank against the gale outside, their white bellies flashing like mica.

A man came up the path three weeks ago, carrying an instrument wrapped in oilcloth. He was a clerk from the water board down in the valley, a young fellow with red knuckles and the hurried, apologetic gait of someone who spends his life among ledgers.

"It belonged to my grandfather," he said, setting the bundle on my workbench. "He kept it in the scullery. Said it told him when the sheep would crowd the hedges. But the column parted. There’s an inch of nothing between the two silver halves, and it won't join, no matter how hard I shake it."

I untied the hemp cord. The case was fruitwood, likely pear, darkened by decades of lard-smoke and peat. Inside lay an old stick tube, pale and cloudy with internal bloom. 

"You must never shake them," I told him, not unkindly. "Air is stubborn. Once a bubble finds its way into the Torricellian vacuum at the top, it treats the void like home. It expands until the weight of the silver means nothing."

He stood by the stove, his coat smelling of wet tweed and coal dust, watching me lift the glass from its brass brackets. 

"Can you draw the air out?" he asked.

"You don't draw it out," I said. "You have to chase it with heat. You have to drive it out with its own nature."

He lingered for an hour, though there was little enough to see. My workshop is not a place of grand machinery. It is a room of small files, corks, mutton tallow, and lengths of narrow rubber tubing. Yet he watched my hands with that peculiar, ravenous attention that modern people reserve for things that do not plug into a socket. He lived in a house where the warmth came through iron radiators at the turn of a valve, where light arrived at the snap of a switch, pure and instantaneous. To him, the mercury was magical precisely because it was stupid. It had no intelligence; it merely obeyed the vast, unpitying bulk of the troposphere.

When I finished resealing the cistern with fresh chamois leather, the young man looked out the window. The tide had gone out, leaving the mud flats ribbed like the palate of a whale. The sun was an orange wafer sinking behind the radar domes on the ridge—those white, golf-ball structures that listen to the upper atmosphere with digital ears, recording data that goes directly to Bracknell or Geneva without ever passing through a human eye.

"They say those things can predict a frost five days out," he murmured.

"They can," I replied, wiping my thumbs on a greasy rag.

"Then what is this for?" He tapped the pearwood frame.

"This doesn't predict five days out," I said. "This tells you what is happening to the room you are standing in. It tells you the weight of the air that is currently resting on your shoulders."

He paid me in crumpled notes, took his heirloom by its brass ring, and walked down the cliff stairs, stepping carefully among the sea-cabbage and loose flint.

After he left, the dusk came on in earnest. I did not light the lamp right away. There is a period between sunset and true dark where the mercury tubes catch the remaining blue from the sea and turn incandescent. They look like seven glowing needles driven into the heart of the house.

I looked at the middle one—an old Negretti & Zambra with a mahogany pediment. The meniscus was convex, round and firm as an acorn. That meant the glass was rising. The storm that had beaten against the headland since Tuesday was flattening out, its spiral uncoiling eastward toward the Baltic, leaving in its wake that thin, icy clarity where every sound carries for miles.

Far out on the shipping lanes, a container vessel was moving south, its deck lights strung out like a village adrift on the black water. Below my floorboards, the timbers of the old cottage creaked as the temperature dropped. The wood shrank; the iron nails groaned against their grain; the earth turned its shoulder to the sun.

We spend our days trying to name the things that press upon us—grief, debt, the passage of a year, the strange, cold certainty that we are growing older in an empty house. We give these burdens names because we think names make them smaller. 

But the air has no name for itself. It simply falls, sixty miles of it, pressing against the glass, waiting for the glass to break. I banked the stove with sea-coal, trimmed the wick of the oil lamp, and sat down to write the evening figure in the log: *1014 millibars. Clear. Wind hauling north-northwest. The glass is steady.*
